arms.name: pooled
arms.note: connections returned to a per-file pool on drop and reused

endpoints: connections actually built for N opens of the same database, counted in the store
daemon CPU milliseconds per entry for a walk of the real mount, the indexer's workload
read syscalls per directory open, which must not regress

connections_built.note: one, not none: the first open finds nothing idle because the account keeper is using its connection rather than resting it.

cpu_ms_per_entry.honest_limit: the 1.28 figure is a single walk, not a median. The factor of four is well outside the pooled arm's own spread, so the direction and rough size hold, but a like-for-like spread for the old arm was never taken.
cpu_ms_per_entry.samples: seven walks of about 4,096 entries each, median reported

measured.fixture: the owner's account on the development machine: 184,092 items, a 564 MB metadata database, an actual kernel FUSE mount, with GNOME's localsearch crawling at about 90 percent of a core throughout -- as it was during the measurement this is compared against.

time_to_settle_after_a_daemon_start.today: 16 to 25 minutes at about 100 percent of a core

prediction.connections_built: today N for N opens; pooled, a handful -- one per worker thread that touches the store, so bounded by the runtime's thread count, not by the operation count.
prediction.cpu_per_entry: 1.28 ms today. An open plus one statement measures 0.10 ms against 0.002 ms warm, and the profile says roughly 13/16 of the CPU is that overhead, so I predict between 0.2 and 0.5 ms -- a factor of three to six, not a factor of fifty. The rest is the listing itself, which pooling does not touch.
prediction.i_may_be_wrong_about: whether the opens are spread across many threads. If each tokio blocking worker takes a different connection, the pool has to hold one per thread and the win is smaller than a single shared connection would give. It also may reveal contention that a fresh connection per operation was hiding.

question: cirrove-service opens a new SQLite connection at 58 call sites, one per operation. Does pooling them per database file remove the open-parse-close cost, and what does a directory listing on the mount cost afterwards?
result: passed. 200 opens build 1 connection instead of 200. 1.28 ms of daemon CPU per entry became 0.32. A daemon start settles in 57 seconds at 16 percent of a core instead of 16 to 25 minutes at 100 percent.
risks_to_check: a connection must never be returned to the pool inside a transaction
:memory: databases must never be pooled -- each open is a separate database and the tests depend on that isolation
the write gate must still serialise writers
the_contract_that_had_to_be_kept: Before pooling, the last Store to drop was the last connection to close, and SQLite retires -wal and -shm when the last connection closes. A pool that outlived its stores left a write-ahead log beside a cleanly closed account, which reads downstream as a crash; three tests said so immediately. Idle connections therefore exist only while at least one store does: the pool counts live stores per database and closes everything when the count reaches zero. The old contract is unchanged.

what_a_start_costs_now.how: /proc/<pid>/stat fields 14+15 over an interval, and per-thread from /proc/<pid>/task/*/stat. `ps` reports a lifetime average and will keep reporting the settle long after it is over, which is how this was misread once already.
what_a_start_costs_now.measured: 2026-09-17 on the owner's machine at b5a725a, with the account ready and 184,170 items indexed across two feeds.
what_a_start_costs_now.not_profiled: the six minutes were not attributed to a call stack. `pkexec` no longer works from the agent's tool channel -- on this date it hung ten minutes waiting for an authentication agent it cannot show and had to be killed by PID -- so Yama's ptrace_scope could not be lowered. The owner can do it in one line: `pkexec sysctl -w kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0`, sample with eu-stack, set it back to 1.
what_a_start_costs_now.settle: about fourteen percent of a core for roughly six minutes, spread evenly across the tokio workers rather than sitting on one, and then 0.72 percent over a minute at fourteen minutes in, with 77 MiB of RSS.
what_a_start_costs_now.why_this_is_recorded_here: the result line above says a start 'settles in 57 seconds at 16 percent of a core', which reads as a steady sixteen percent forever. It is not: sixteen percent is the settle, and what follows it is under one percent. The row this record belongs to is about the defect that made a start cost 16 to 25 minutes at 100 percent, and the thing left after it is a six-minute settle rather than a drain.

what_the_prediction_missed: It said nothing about the state a reused connection carries, and that was the whole difficulty. Three kinds turned up, each found by a test rather than by reading the code: an open transaction; six temporary tables that directory publication creates without IF NOT EXISTS, on purpose, so that finding them already there is a failure rather than a silent inheritance; and a progress handler that capacity::cold installs to abandon a fetch, which interrupted whoever got the connection next with SQLITE_INTERRUPT. A connection now goes back only if it is in the state a fresh one would be in, and is closed otherwise. The risks_to_check list named the transaction and the in-memory isolation and missed both of the others.
where_the_prediction_was_right: 0.2 to 0.5 ms per entry was predicted and 0.32 was measured. The reasoning behind it also held: pooling removes the open-parse-close overhead and leaves the listing itself, so this was never going to be the factor of fifty that a single warm statement suggests.
why_it_matters: Profiling the daemon on 2026-09-16 put 13 of 16 computing stacks in Store::open (schema read), sqlite3Prepare/yy_reduce (parsing SQL) and closing a connection, and only 4 in Store::with_children, the work that was asked for. A desktop file indexer re-checking the mount costs 1.28 ms of daemon CPU per file, about a thousand times what a local disk costs, so a legitimate re-check becomes a quarter of an hour of fan noise. ADR 0006 called a pooled read connection a prerequisite, not an optimisation.
